title: Indian-Origin Texas Lab Owner on US Fugitive List Over $93M Medicare Fraud
excerpt: Khadeer Khan Mohammed, 46, is accused of billing Medicare $93 million for genetic tests doctors never ordered; HHS investigators say the alleged fugitive may be in Hyderabad, India.
body:
• The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Office of Inspector General has named Khadeer Khan Mohammed, 46, a fugitive over an alleged $93 million Medicare fraud scheme run through his Richardson, Texas laboratory.
  • Between August 2023 and October 2024, American Premier Labs LLC allegedly submitted about $93 million in Medicare claims for genetic tests; the program paid out at least $65 million, including roughly $13 million in a single 10-day window in 2023.
  • Investigators say physicians' personal information was used without their knowledge to make claims appear medically authorised. The tests were never ordered by those doctors and never used in patient care.
  • Mohammed is believed to have fled to Hyderabad, India. Federal officials have seized nearly $6 million from bank accounts linked to him, and the hunt for him continues.

U.S. federal authorities have named Khadeer Khan Mohammed, a 46-year-old Indian-origin laboratory owner, a fugitive in connection with an alleged $93 million Medicare fraud scheme, saying they believe he has fled to Hyderabad, India, to evade arrest. The designation by the Department of Health and Human Services' Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG) marks one of the larger recent cases in an ongoing federal crackdown on fraudulent genetic-testing claims billed to the government's health insurance program for older Americans.

Context & Background: The Alleged Scheme

According to federal officials cited in multiple reports, Mohammed owned American Premier Labs LLC, based in Richardson, Texas. Between August 2023 and October 2024, the laboratory allegedly submitted, or directed others to submit, approximately $93 million in Medicare claims for genetic testing services that authorities describe as ineligible for reimbursement.

The mechanics of the scheme, as described by investigators, relied on borrowing other people's credentials. Federal officials say physicians' personal identifying information was used without their knowledge or consent to submit claims for genetic tests performed on Medicare beneficiaries with whom those physicians had no treatment relationship.

"These tests were not ordered by the physicians and were not used in the care of the beneficiaries."

— U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, statement

In other words, doctors listed on the paperwork reportedly never ordered the tests, were unaware their identities were being used, and the results played no role in any patient's treatment. Genetic testing fraud has become a recurring target for federal prosecutors because each claim can be worth hundreds of dollars, and tests billed in bulk can generate enormous payouts before the fraud is detected. In Mohammed's case, Medicare allegedly paid about $13 million in a single 10-day period in 2023 alone, and at least $65 million across the life of the scheme.

The criminal investigation was led by the FBI's Dallas Field Office together with HHS-OIG, and charges were filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, where an arrest warrant has been issued.

Impact & Analysis: The Money and the Manhunt

The immediate financial damage is measurable. Medicare paid at least $65 million on claims authorities now call fraudulent, and federal officials have seized nearly $6 million from bank accounts linked to Mohammed. Those seizures matter: in healthcare fraud cases, prosecutors routinely move early to freeze assets so defendants cannot spend or move the proceeds before a verdict.

The harder part is custody. Authorities believe Mohammed fled the United States after charges were filed and is now in Hyderabad, in the Indian state of Telangana. U.S. officials have indicated they will pursue extradition if local authorities can confirm his whereabouts, according to reports in the Telugu press. Extradition between India and the United States is possible under a bilateral treaty, but such cases move slowly — locating the suspect is only the first hurdle, followed by foreign arrest procedures, legal challenges in Indian courts, and diplomatic coordination.

The fugitive listing itself is also a tactic. HHS-OIG maintains a public most-wanted list for healthcare fraud fugitives, and the publicity is designed to generate tips. Past cases show that once a suspect is listed, enforcement often depends on someone recognizing the name or face.

Diaspora Angle

Cases like this land awkwardly in the Indian-American community, which is heavily represented in the healthcare and life-sciences fields — the very sectors this alleged fraud exploited. An Indian-origin name on a U.S. federal fugitive list draws outsized attention relative to the community's share of such crimes, and community leaders have long noted that high-profile fraud cases can colour perceptions of a diaspora otherwise known for its outsized contributions to American medicine. The allegations remain just that — allegations — and Mohammed is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. But the Hyderabad angle, with investigators pointing to the city as his suspected hiding place, adds a cross-border dimension that keeps the case squarely in Indian media coverage as well.

What's Next

The immediate question is whether Indian authorities can locate Mohammed in Hyderabad. If confirmed and detained, extradition proceedings could begin, though similar cases have taken years to resolve. If convicted in the Northern District of Texas, he would face prison time and restitution orders on top of the asset seizures already underway.

Beyond this case, federal officials have signaled that genetic-testing billing fraud remains an enforcement priority, with HHS-OIG continuing to target laboratories that bill for medically unnecessary tests. For Medicare's trust funds, each conviction and each dollar clawed back is a small but tangible win in a program that processes trillions in claims.
